name: Bake Element Resistance
purpose: Verify bake element continuity and resistance to rule out open or shorted element on no-bake-heat complaints.
failureModes: Open (OL): no bake heat, common failure point (visible burn/blister often present)
Reading well outside range or grounded to chassis: shorted/damaged element
testingTips: Disconnect power before testing at element terminals
Use nameplate wattage with Ohm's law (R = V²/W) to sanity-check if spec unknown — common bake elements run 2000-3000W at 240V
notes: Verify model spec — wattage/resistance varies by oven cavity size and element design

name: Broil Element Resistance
purpose: Verify broil element continuity and resistance to rule out open or shorted element on no-broil-heat complaints.
failureModes: Open (OL): no broil heat, common failure point (visible burn/blister often present)
Reading well outside range or grounded to chassis: shorted/damaged element
testingTips: Disconnect power before testing at element terminals
Use nameplate wattage with Ohm's law (R = V²/W) to sanity-check if spec unknown — common broil elements run 2500-3600W at 240V
notes: Verify model spec — wattage/resistance varies by oven cavity size and element design

name: Convection Fan Motor Amperage
purpose: Confirm convection fan motor runs and draws expected current during convection bake/roast cycles.
failureModes: Zero amps: seized motor, open winding, control not energizing motor
High amps: motor binding/dragging on debris, bearing failure
testingTips: Clamp meter on motor lead during an active convection cycle
Check for grease/debris buildup on fan blade before condemning motor
notes: Verify against motor nameplate rating when available

name: Oven Temperature Sensor (RTD) Resistance
purpose: Verify oven RTD temperature probe resistance at room temp to rule out drift or failure causing temp inaccuracy or error codes.
failureModes: Open (OL): sensor failure — often triggers an F-code and locks out bake/broil
Reading far outside range at room temp: sensor drift — can cause food to over/undercook despite display showing correct set temp
testingTips: Test with oven fully cooled to room temperature for the baseline reading
Resistance rises roughly linearly with temperature (PTC/RTD behavior) — many common ranges spec ~1080Ω at ~75°F rising toward ~1200Ω near 500°F, but confirm against exact model spec
notes: ~1080-1100Ω at room temp is a common industry approximation across many electric range brands, but exact spec/curve varies — verify against manufacturer chart when precision matters

name: Ice Maker Module Motor Amperage
purpose: Confirm ice maker gear motor draws expected current during a harvest/ejection cycle.
failureModes: Zero amps during harvest: open motor winding, failed module control board
High amps or stalling: ice jam in tray, frozen ejector, worn/stripped gears
testingTips: Clamp meter during a manually initiated harvest cycle (most modules have a test button/lever)
Listen/feel for stalling vs. free rotation — a stalled motor often draws higher current briefly then trips thermal protection
notes: Verify against module nameplate/spec when available — varies by icemaker module design

name: Ice Maker Water Fill Valve Coil Resistance
purpose: Verify ice maker fill valve solenoid coil continuity when tray fails to fill after a harvest cycle.
failureModes: Open (OL): failed solenoid coil, no fill water reaching tray
Very low reading: shorted coil
testingTips: Test at valve connector with power disconnected
Rule out low household water pressure and kinked/frozen fill tube before condemning valve
notes: May be a dedicated icemaker valve or a shared valve with additional dishwasher/refrigerator door dispenser circuits — confirm which coil you're testing

name: Ice Maker Mold Thermostat Continuity
purpose: Verify mold thermostat closes (near-zero resistance) once ice reaches harvest temperature, enabling the harvest cycle.
failureModes: Stays open (OL) even when ice is fully frozen: failed thermostat, harvest cycle never triggers
Closed at warm ambient (should be open): failed thermostat, may cause premature/incorrect harvest attempts
testingTips: Test at connector; for a true pass/fail check, verify state changes as tray temp crosses the rated trip point (often near 15-18°F on many designs)
Bimetal thermostats are typically not adjustable — a bad reading means replacement, not calibration
notes: Trip temperature and continuity behavior vary by manufacturer — verify against spec when precision matters

name: Ice Maker Harvest Heater Resistance
purpose: Verify harvest heater continuity on models that use a small heater (rather than a gear-driven twist tray) to release ice from the mold.
failureModes: Open (OL): no release heat, ice sticks in tray/mold
Shorted/very low reading: damaged element
testingTips: Disconnect power before testing at heater terminals
Confirm your unit design actually uses a harvest heater vs. a twist-tray gear motor before testing this ID
notes: Only applicable to heater-release style icemakers — verify design and spec by model

name: Electric Dryer Heating Element Resistance
purpose: Verify heating element continuity and resistance to rule out open or shorted element on no-heat complaints.
failureModes: Open (OL): no heat, most common cause of a no-heat/long-dry-time complaint on electric dryers
Reading well outside range or grounded to cabinet: shorted/damaged element
testingTips: Disconnect power before testing at element terminals
Use nameplate wattage with Ohm's law (R = V²/W) to sanity-check if spec unknown — common elements run ~5000-5600W at 240V
notes: Verify model spec — wattage/resistance varies by brand and dryer capacity

name: Dryer Thermal Fuse Continuity
purpose: Verify thermal fuse continuity — this is a one-time safety fuse that opens permanently if the dryer overheats.
failureModes: Open (OL): fuse has tripped — no heat and often no tumble on some models until replaced
A tripped fuse is a symptom, not a root cause — inspect venting/lint path and cycling thermostat before replacing fuse alone
testingTips: Disconnect power before testing at fuse terminals
Always diagnose and clear the airflow restriction (clogged vent, lint) that caused the trip, or the new fuse will blow again

name: Dryer Cycling Thermostat Continuity
purpose: Verify cycling thermostat contacts close at room/cool temp (bimetal switch), allowing heat circuit to complete.
failureModes: Open (OL) at room/cool temp: failed thermostat — no heat or heat cycles incorrectly
Stays closed regardless of temp: failed thermostat — can contribute to overheating/scorching complaints
testingTips: Test at room temperature with unit cooled down and disconnected from power
Several thermostats of different trip points may exist on one unit (operating, high-limit, cycling) — identify which one you're testing
notes: Trip point varies by thermostat's rated function and position in the airflow path — verify part number/spec before replacing

name: Dryer Drum Motor Winding Resistance
purpose: Verify drum motor winding continuity when drum fails to turn or motor hums without turning.
failureModes: Open (OL) on main or start winding: failed motor
Motor hums but drum doesn't turn: often a mechanical issue (belt, idler pulley) rather than winding — check both before replacing motor
testingTips: Disconnect motor connector and power before testing
Also check centrifugal switch continuity (if equipped) since a failed switch can mimic a bad winding symptom
notes: Universal-motor designs read low resistance and vary by brand — verify against manufacturer spec when known

name: Gas Flame Sensor (Rectification) Current
purpose: Verify flame-sensing (flame rectification) DC microamp signal is present and adequate once burner lights, confirming the control will hold the gas valve open.
failureModes: No microamp signal with flame present: dirty/degraded sensor rod, poor ground/bond, or failed control board sensing circuit — valve may open then shut down shortly after ignition
Low but present signal: partially degraded sensor rod (carbon buildup) or flame not fully contacting rod — often intermittent shutdown symptom
testingTips: Use a microamp meter in series with the sensor wire per the specific control board's test procedure — this is a live-flame, powered test, use appropriate caution
Clean the flame sensor rod of carbon/oxide buildup before condemning the control board
notes: This applies to flame-rectification style sensing used on some gas range/oven ignition systems — not all designs use this method; confirm ignition system type before applying
